source: reports/higs-trainability-implementation.md rounds 1-27, benchmark results on EPIC-05 A100

measurement_config.notes: Frozen topology; measurements are means over 20 steps

speedup_ratios.notes: HiGS faster across all metrics; -15.6% total, -13.9% train
HiGS faster; -13.5% total, -11.8% train; forward near parity, backward -18.9%
Speedup holds at B=1; -12.7% total, -12.1% train
Similar speedup at B=4; -12.2% total, -12.2% train

vs_gaussian_count.trend: FLAT (slight decrease at higher N; -2% total speedup)
vs_gaussian_count.interpretation: Speedup does NOT increase with N; consistent across LOW and HIGH

vs_resolution.trend: FLAT (slight decrease at higher res; -1% total speedup)
vs_resolution.interpretation: Speedup does NOT increase with resolution

vs_culling_ratio.trend: WEAK_NEGATIVE (speedup slightly lower with higher culling)
vs_culling_ratio.interpretation: Contradicts H4 (culling-dependent); higher culling does NOT increase speedup

speedup_source.primary: Elimination of std's indexing_backward (~9.8 ms) and visible-subset gather costs
speedup_source.secondary: Native backward kernels avoid pipeline re-execution (vs gsplat_recompute)
speedup_source.tertiary: Small kernel-level improvements (SH VJP, projection VJP optimization rounds 8, 13, 25)
speedup_source.not_from: Culling does NOT reduce blend_bwd work (culled Gaussians generate zero isects anyway)

higs_forward.visible_subset_projection: Second projection over visible subset (~0.6 ms)
higs_forward.gather: Native gather kernel (~0.9 ms for visible subset)
higs_forward.culling_mask: Union visibility mask computation (~0.14 ms after fused mask optimization)

speedup_source.primary: Native gather kernel avoids PyTorch's pathological index_select for wide rows
speedup_source.secondary: Fused union visibility mask eliminates double reduction
speedup_source.neutral: Visible-subset raster saves ~10.4 ms but gather+2nd projection costs ~11.8 ms (net ~parity)
speedup_source.conclusion: Forward is near parity; the win is almost entirely from backward

key_findings.H1_scaling: NOT_SUPPORTED - Speedup does not increase with workload (N, resolution, batch)
key_findings.H2_backward_dominates: SUPPORTED - Backward provides the speedup; forward is at parity
key_findings.H4_culling_dependent: WEAKLY_REFUTED - Higher culling does not increase speedup

overall_conclusion.primary_finding: Trainable HiGS native provides consistent ~13-16% training speedup (S_FB ~1.16-1.18x) across LOW and HIGH workload, but speedup does NOT increase with scale
overall_conclusion.mechanism: Speedup comes from backward (elimination of indexing_backward + native kernels), not from forward culling or hierarchical rendering
overall_conclusion.scaling_behavior: FLAT - speedup is workload-independent in the tested range (1M-6M Gaussians, 540p-1080p, B1-B4)
overall_conclusion.implication: H1 (increasing benefit with scale) is NOT supported by evidence; HiGS advantage is architectural (backward efficiency) rather than scaling-dependent
